lessons.title: Lab: Mock technical interview - Windows Server Administrator

story.title: Interview day for Windows Server Administrator

scenes.text: Asha has a Windows Server Administrator interview at 11 a.m. She has studied, but worries about being asked something she cannot answer.
Her mentor says: 'Think aloud, be honest about gaps, and give real examples.'

steps.title: What this round tests
steps.body: Active Directory, Group Policy, DNS/DHCP, patching, backups and troubleshooting on Windows Server.

steps.title: How to answer
steps.body: Start with a one-line direct answer, then give the reasoning, a real example and a trade-off. Interviewers listen for how you think, not only the final answer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Memorised definitions with no example, bluffing past gaps, and talking for five minutes without structure.

rounds.q: A user says they cannot log in and gets 'account locked out'. How do you investigate?
points: find the source of bad passwords via event 4740 on the DC
check stale credentials, mapped drives, services
rounds.model: I confirm the lockout in Active Directory Users and Computers, then find the lockout source from event ID 4740 on the PDC emulator, which shows the calling computer. Usually it is a saved credential, a mapped drive, a phone with old email password or a service running under the user. I unlock the account, remove or update the stale credential, and tell the user. If it repeats I look for password spraying.
followups: Which DC holds the lockout detail first?

rounds.q: Explain how Group Policy is applied and how you troubleshoot a policy not applying.
rounds.model: Policies apply in order Local, Site, Domain, OU, with later ones winning unless a higher one is enforced. If a policy is missing I run gpresult /r or gpresult /h on the client, check security filtering, WMI filters, block inheritance and whether the computer can reach a DC and SYSVOL. I also verify SYSVOL/DFSR replication is healthy.
followups: Difference between loopback merge and replace?

rounds.q: What are the FSMO roles and what happens if a role holder fails?
rounds.model: The five are Schema Master and Domain Naming Master (forest-wide), and PDC Emulator, RID Master and Infrastructure Master (per domain). I transfer roles gracefully when a DC is being retired. If the holder is permanently lost I seize the role with ntdsutil or PowerShell and never bring the old DC back online. PDC Emulator failure is noticed first because of time sync and password changes.
followups: Which role matters most day to day?

rounds.q: How do you patch a fleet of Windows servers safely?
rounds.model: I use WSUS, Configuration Manager or Azure Update Manager with rings: test, then non-critical, then critical servers. Patching occurs in agreed windows, with a snapshot or backup first, cluster nodes patched one by one, and post-patch validation of services. Failed patches are rolled back and tracked in a change record.
followups: How do you patch a domain controller?

rounds.q: DNS is working for some clients but not others. How do you narrow it down?
points: nslookup from affected and good clients
check DNS server settings and scope options
rounds.model: I compare nslookup results from a good and bad client against the same DNS server, check what DNS servers the client gets from DHCP, then verify the records exist on each DNS server. Differences point to replication, stale or duplicate records, or a wrong scope option. I also check forwarders and the firewall for port 53.
followups: What does ipconfig /flushdns not fix?

tips: Answer in a clear structure: context, action, result.
Use real examples from your own work, study or projects.
Say what you don't know honestly and show how you'd find out.

quiz.q: Which command shows the Group Policy settings actually applied to a client?
quiz.why: gpresult reports applied GPOs; gpupdate only refreshes them.

quiz.q: Which event ID commonly records an account lockout on a domain controller?
quiz.why: 4740 is 'A user account was locked out'.

quiz.q: In the STAR method for a behavioural answer, what does the 'R' stand for?
options: Result - what happened and what you learned
Reference - who can vouch for you
quiz.why: STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result. Always close with an outcome, ideally measurable, and what you learned.

story.title: A problem lands on your desk

scenes.text: A realistic problem from daily Windows Server Administrator work is described to you, with incomplete information.
The interviewer wants to see calm, structured thinking, safe actions and clear communication.

steps.title: Scenario answers have a shape
steps.body: Clarify and scope -> list hypotheses or options -> act safely, least risky first -> communicate -> verify -> prevent recurrence or improve.

steps.title: What interviewers listen for
steps.body: Do you ask questions before acting? Do you think about impact on people, customers and safety? Do you know when to escalate?

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Jumping to a fix without diagnosis, ignoring communication, and claiming nothing ever goes wrong.

rounds.q: A file server's shared drive is 'very slow' for the finance team at month end.
points: check open files, antivirus, backup running
rounds.model: I clarify who and since when, then check performance counters: disk queue, latency, CPU, memory, network. I look at what runs at month end: backups, antivirus scans, a large report. I fix the contention, such as rescheduling the backup, and document the change. If capacity is the cause I raise a request for storage or tiering.
followups: How do you prove the backup is the cause?

rounds.q: Your domain controller shows replication errors in dcdiag.
points: do not force or seize blindly
rounds.model: I run repadmin /replsummary and /showrepl, dcdiag /test:dns, and check time sync and ports. Most replication failures come from DNS or connectivity. I fix the root cause rather than forcing replication, check for lingering objects and the tombstone lifetime, and inform the team before touching production DCs.
followups: What is the tombstone lifetime?

rounds.q: A critical server will not boot after patching at 2 AM.
points: safe mode, last known good, boot logs
rounds.model: I raise a P1, inform stakeholders, and check the console for the stop code. I try safe mode or recovery to uninstall the update, otherwise restore from the pre-patch snapshot or backup. After recovery I validate services and write a review covering why the test ring missed it.
followups: Who approves a rollback?

rounds.q: You strongly disagree with your manager's decision on how to do a piece of work. What do you do?
points: commit if overruled, escalate only for ethics or safety
rounds.model: I'd ask to understand the reasoning first, then share my concern privately with data and an alternative. If after listening the manager still decides otherwise, I commit and execute well, unless the decision is unethical or unsafe, in which case I escalate through the proper channel. I'd also record the risk so we can review later.
followups: What if you were proved right later?

rounds.q: You notice, after delivery, an error in your own work that nobody has noticed yet. What do you do?
rounds.model: I'd assess the impact quickly, tell my lead and affected people right away with a proposed fix, and correct it. Then I'd add a check or review step so it doesn't recur. Hiding it would turn a small error into a trust problem.
followups: What if telling would delay a big launch?

tips: Answer in a clear structure: context, action, result.
Use real examples from your own work, study or projects.
Say what you don't know honestly and show how you'd find out.

quiz.why: Schema and Domain Naming masters exist once per forest.

quiz.q: What is the safest action if the original holder of an FSMO role is permanently lost?
options: Seize the role on another DC and never reconnect the old one
quiz.why: Seizing is for permanent loss; the old DC must not return with stale roles.

quiz.q: An interviewer asks something you do not know. The best response is to:
options: Bluff confidently so you look senior
Stay silent until they move on
Change the subject to your strengths
Say you are not sure, share the closest related thing you do know and how you would find out
quiz.why: Honest reasoning beats bluffing; interviewers probe bluffs quickly and value learning ability.

lessons.title: Lab: Behavioural & HR round - Windows Server Administrator

scenes.text: The technical rounds went well. Now the HR manager meets you for the Windows Server Administrator role.
Questions about yourself, mistakes, conflict, money and notice period decide the offer as much as skills.

steps.title: Use STAR
steps.body: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Keep the example real, specific and about 90 seconds.

steps.title: Salary and offers
steps.body: Research market ranges, discuss the whole package, be honest about notice period and other offers. Never invent a competing offer. Read the offer letter fully before signing.

steps.title: Be yourself, prepared
steps.body: Replace every [bracketed] gap in the model answers with your own true story. Interviewers can tell a script from a lived example.

rounds.q: Tell me about yourself.
rounds.model: I'm a Windows Server Administrator candidate with [X years/study background]. Recently I [specific achievement with a number or outcome], and before that I [earlier relevant work]. I enjoy [the part of the work you really like], and this role fits because [specific reason tied to the company]. I would like to contribute on [area] while growing in [skill].
followups: Which part of that are you proudest of?

rounds.q: Describe a time you failed or made a serious mistake at work or in your studies.
rounds.model: Pick a real, moderate failure. Example shape: 'I [mistake] which caused [impact]. I told my lead the same day, helped fix it, and wrote a checklist so it could not recur. Since then [evidence it stuck].' Avoid fake weaknesses such as 'I work too hard'.
followups: What would you do differently today?

rounds.q: Tell me about a conflict with a colleague and how you resolved it.
rounds.model: I described the issue privately and factually, asked for their view, and we found we were optimising for different goals. We agreed a shared target and a way to review it. The outcome was [result], and we still work well together. I escalated only when we could not agree after trying directly.
followups: When would you escalate to a manager?

rounds.q: Why are you leaving your current job, or why did you choose this career?
rounds.model: I have learned a lot in my current role, and I now want [bigger scope / different domain / deeper skills], which this role offers. I'm not leaving because of conflict; I'm moving towards [specific thing]. Freshers: 'I chose this field because [real reason] and I have prepared by [projects, practice].'
followups: What would make you leave this company too?

rounds.q: What are your salary expectations?
rounds.model: I've researched this role and city and see a range of roughly [your researched range]. Based on my experience I'm looking at the upper half, but I'm flexible on the structure of the package and interested mainly in the right role and growth. Could you share the band for this position?
followups: Is that negotiable if we offer a lower base with bonus?

rounds.q: What is your notice period, and can you join earlier?
rounds.model: My contractual notice period is [N days]. I can ask my manager about early release or a buyout, but I cannot promise it. I will keep you updated honestly and ensure a proper handover.
followups: Would you serve the full notice if needed?

tips: Write 5 true stories (success, failure, conflict, pressure, leadership) and reuse them.
Never criticise a former employer.
Ask for the salary band if you are unsure.

quiz.q: Asked 'What is your salary expectation?' early in the process, a sensible approach is to:
options: Research the market range for the role and city, then give a range or ask about the band for the role
Quote the highest number you can imagine
quiz.why: Preparation with market data keeps you credible and leaves room to negotiate.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to explain a gap in your CV?
options: State it briefly and honestly, say what you did or learned, and move to why you are ready now
quiz.why: Short, honest and forward-looking. Falsified dates are found in background verification and can cost the offer.

quiz.q: Why should you research the company before an interview?
options: Only to memorise the founder's name
It is unnecessary if you are skilled
To tailor examples to their products, customers and challenges, and to ask informed questions
quiz.why: Relevant, specific answers show real interest and fit.

Her mentor says: 'Think aloud, be honest about gaps, and give real examples.'

steps.title: What this round tests
steps.body: Linux troubleshooting, users and permissions, systemd, storage, networking, security hardening and automation.

steps.title: How to answer
steps.body: Start with a one-line direct answer, then give the reasoning, a real example and a trade-off. Interviewers listen for how you think, not only the final answer.

steps.title: Common mistakes

rounds.q: A server's root disk is 100% full at 2 AM. Walk me through what you do.
points: logs, journal, deleted-but-open files via lsof
don't delete blindly; fix and prevent
rounds.model: I run df -h and df -i to see space and inodes, then du -xh --max-depth=1 down the largest path. Common causes are runaway logs, core dumps or a deleted file still held open, which lsof +L1 reveals. I compress or truncate safely, restart the holding process if needed, and add log rotation and monitoring so it does not recur. I record it as an incident.
followups: What if it is /var/log/journal?

rounds.q: Explain Linux file permissions, including setuid and the sticky bit.
points: sticky bit on shared dirs like /tmp
rounds.model: Each file has read, write, execute bits for owner, group and others, written as 755 or rwxr-xr-x. Setuid makes an executable run with its owner's privileges (like passwd), so it is a security-sensitive bit. The sticky bit on a shared directory such as /tmp lets users delete only their own files. ACLs extend this when groups are not enough.
followups: How do you find setuid files?

rounds.q: A systemd service fails to start. How do you debug?
rounds.model: I run systemctl status for the failure reason, then journalctl -u name -b for logs. I check the unit file, environment, working directory and dependencies, then run the ExecStart command manually as the service user. After fixing I daemon-reload and restart.
followups: What does Restart=on-failure do?

rounds.q: How would you extend an LVM logical volume holding /var by 20 GB online?
rounds.model: I check vgs/lvs for free space; if none I add a disk, pvcreate and vgextend. Then lvextend -L +20G with the resize option or follow with xfs_growfs or resize2fs. I verify with df -h. I would have a recent backup and check that the filesystem supports online grow (XFS grows but cannot shrink).
followups: Can you shrink XFS?

rounds.q: How do you harden SSH on a production server?
points: key auth, disable password and root login
restrict users and ports with firewall
rounds.model: I disable password and direct root login, use key-based or certificate auth with MFA where possible, restrict AllowUsers or groups, limit source IPs in the firewall, keep OpenSSH patched and monitor auth logs. I test a second session before reloading sshd so I do not lock myself out.
followups: Why keep a second session open?

tips: Answer in a clear structure: context, action, result.
Use real examples from your own work, study or projects.
Say what you don't know honestly and show how you'd find out.

quiz.why: df -i reports inode usage; a disk can be 'full' by inodes with free space remaining.

quiz.q: A file shows -rwsr-xr-x. What does the 's' mean?
options: setuid is set; it runs with the owner's privileges
quiz.why: The s in the owner execute position is setuid.

options: Result - what happened and what you learned
Reference - who can vouch for you
quiz.why: STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result. Always close with an outcome, ideally measurable, and what you learned.

rounds.q: Explain vMotion, DRS and HA and how they differ.
points: HA restarts VMs after host failure
rounds.model: vMotion moves a running VM between hosts without downtime. DRS uses vMotion to balance CPU and memory across a cluster and respects affinity rules. followups: What does 'consolidation needed' mean?

scenes.text: Asha has a Network Engineer interview at 11 a.m. She has studied, but worries about being asked something she cannot answer.
Her mentor says: 'Think aloud, be honest about gaps, and give real examples.'

steps.title: What this round tests
steps.body: TCP/IP, routing and switching, VLANs, OSPF/BGP basics, firewalls, NAT, troubleshooting methodology.

steps.title: How to answer
steps.body: Start with a one-line direct answer, then give the reasoning, a real example and a trade-off. Interviewers listen for how you think, not only the final answer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Memorised definitions with no example, bluffing past gaps, and talking for five minutes without structure.

rounds.q: Walk me through what happens when you type a URL into a browser, at the network level.
rounds.model: The browser resolves the name through DNS, then the host determines whether the destination is local (ARP for MAC) or via the default gateway. A TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) opens the connection, TLS negotiates keys and certificates, then HTTP request and response flow. Routers forward hop by hop, NAT may rewrite addresses.
followups: Where would a firewall interfere?

rounds.q: Explain VLANs, trunking and inter-VLAN routing.
rounds.model: A VLAN is a logical broadcast domain. Access ports carry one untagged VLAN, trunks carry many using 802.1Q tags. Different VLANs need a Layer 3 device: a router subinterface or switch SVI, to route between them.
followups: What is the native VLAN risk?

rounds.q: Compare OSPF and BGP and when each is used.
rounds.model: OSPF is a link-state interior protocol using areas and cost, fast convergence inside an organisation. BGP is the path-vector protocol between autonomous systems and is policy-driven, used for internet and large data-centre fabrics.
followups: What is an OSPF DR?

rounds.q: How does spanning tree prevent loops and what is a common failure?
rounds.model: STP elects a root bridge and blocks redundant paths so there is a loop-free tree. Edge ports use PortFast with BPDU Guard. Problems include an unplanned switch becoming root or a topology-change storm, which I handle by setting root priority deliberately.
followups: RSTP versus STP?

rounds.q: Explain NAT and the difference between SNAT, DNAT and PAT.
rounds.model: NAT rewrites addresses at a boundary. SNAT changes the source, DNAT changes the destination such as publishing a server, and PAT maps many private hosts to one public IP using ports. The firewall keeps a state table to translate return traffic.

rounds.q: Explain the shared responsibility model.

rounds.q: How do you design a highly available web application in the cloud?

rounds.q: Explain IAM best practices.

rounds.q: How do you control and reduce cloud cost?

rounds.q: Explain ACID properties.
rounds.model: Atomicity: a transaction is all or nothing. Consistency: it moves the database between valid states. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see partial work. Durability: committed data survives crashes, via logs.
followups: Isolation levels?

rounds.q: A query suddenly became slow. How do you diagnose?
rounds.model: I look at the execution plan, compare with the previous one, check stale statistics, missing or unused indexes, parameter sniffing, blocking and recent deployments. I fix the cause and verify.

rounds.q: Describe your backup and recovery strategy.

rounds.q: Clustered vs non-clustered index?

items.q: What tools have you used?

items.q: How do you stay updated?
